paragraphs: Agent Reviewers addresses a practical gap in scientific writing: many manuscripts receive too little external feedback to support revision. The paper builds an automated review system around several language-model agents that imitate aspects of human reviewing. Its purpose is to produce detailed, professional feedback that authors can use while refining a paper.

The authors first collect historical open-access papers and their reviews, then use a language model to standardize the material. They describe the resulting review dataset as the largest compiled to date. The system also includes multimodal reviewers that examine visual elements, extending feedback beyond text. A shared memory pool holds metadata about earlier papers and supplies agents with background knowledge from different research fields.

On ICLR 2024 papers, the system performs better than the existing AI review systems included in the evaluation. Ablation studies support the usefulness of its individual modules and agents. Together, these findings support combining specialized reviewers, visual analysis, and shared research context within an automated feedback process.
icml-2025-agent-reviewers-domain-specifi.tldr: Agent Reviewers combines specialized multimodal agents and shared paper metadata to improve automated scientific feedback.

paragraphs: A calibrated classifier should express confidence that matches how often its predictions are correct. This paper argues that ordinary one-hot labels provide inadequate supervision for that goal: they identify a class with full certainty but offer little information about degrees of ambiguity. Obtaining real images with useful numerical uncertainty annotations is also difficult because suitable uncertain examples are scarce.

Calibration-aware Semantic Mixing, or CSM, addresses this data problem using diffusion models. It generates images that combine characteristics of different classes and assigns them distinct confidence values. The aim is to train with examples that explicitly represent uncertainty, so calibration can draw on richer information than a single categorical label provides.

The method also addresses a mismatch between the intended mixing ratio and the confidence annotation during diffusion generation through calibrated reannotation. The authors investigate loss functions suited to this richer label format. Experiments report better calibration than the state-of-the-art approaches compared, supporting synthetic uncertainty supervision as a useful ingredient in calibration.
icml-2025-beyond-one-hot-labels-semantic.tldr: CSM improves model calibration by generating images with mixed class characteristics and explicit uncertainty annotations.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking learns to order examples so that positive cases rank above negative ones, with performance measured by area under the ROC curve. The usual formulation assumes one binary target. This paper studies what happens when several binary labels are available for each example, such as judgments from different human annotators, but the system must still produce one ranking.

The authors compare two ways to combine that supervision. Loss aggregation combines the objectives associated with the different labels, while label aggregation combines the labels themselves. They characterize the Bayes-optimal solutions for both approaches, examining the rankings each method favors at the population level.

Both approaches can produce Pareto-optimal solutions, meaning that improving performance for one label would require sacrificing performance for another. Yet loss aggregation can still let one label dominate the resulting ranking, a phenomenon the paper calls label dictatorship. This shows why Pareto optimality alone does not rule out undesirable favoritism. The analysis suggests that label aggregation can be preferable, and the experiments support that conclusion.
icml-2025-bipartite-ranking-from-multipl.tldr: Combining ranking losses can unintentionally favor one label, making label aggregation a preferable option in the studied setting.

paragraphs: This paper reexamines whether graph Transformers need to outperform classic message-passing networks on tasks that predict properties of whole graphs. Graph Transformers use global attention, which can potentially address difficulties with long-range relationships. The authors investigate whether older graph neural networks have been underestimated when compared without a sufficiently strong collection of supporting techniques.

Their GNN+ framework combines six established ingredients: edge features, normalization, dropout, residual connections, feed-forward networks, and positional encoding. They apply this framework to GCN, GIN, and GatedGCN, then systematically evaluate the enhanced models on 14 graph-level datasets. The central contribution is a stronger treatment of familiar architectures using widely used components.

Across these evaluations, the enhanced classic networks match or exceed graph Transformer performance, achieve top-three rankings on every dataset, and take first place on eight. They also run several times faster on many datasets. These results challenge the assumption that complex global-attention mechanisms are essential for strong graph-level prediction and establish more competitive classic GNN baselines.
icml-2025-can-classic-gnns-be-strong-bas.tldr: GNN+ equips classic graph networks with established techniques, matching or beating graph Transformers across 14 datasets with greater efficiency.

paragraphs: Constrained Exploitability Descent, or CED, learns strategies for adversarial Markov games from an existing dataset without building an environment model. It combines exploitability descent with policy constraints from offline reinforcement learning. The authors argue that these constraints can be less harmful in adversarial games, where an optimal solution may randomize among actions, than in single-agent problems with optimal pure strategies.

The theoretical guarantees depend on uniform dataset coverage and deterministic, two-player, zero-sum Markov games. Under those conditions, CED converges to a stationary point, and the minimizing player's policy there has the stated mixed-strategy Nash-equilibrium property. The approach also avoids the generalized gradient used by the compared model-based exploitability-descent method.

Experiments find equilibrium policies for the minimizing player when uniform coverage holds and report lower NashConv than a pessimism-based method. Under non-uniform coverage, CED can still progressively improve the behavior policy. With neural networks, it also outperforms behavior cloning and offline self-play in a large two-team robotic combat game.
icml-2025-constrained-exploitability-des.tldr: CED combines offline policy constraints with exploitability descent, with equilibrium-related guarantees under uniform coverage in deterministic two-player zero-sum games.

paragraphs: Predicting a molecule's Hamiltonian matrix supports the calculation of many molecular properties. Equivariant graph neural networks have performed well at this task, but their high-order tensor-product operations are expensive. That computational burden becomes particularly restrictive for large molecular systems and extensive basis sets, motivating a way to reduce the work these networks perform.

SPHNet introduces adaptive sparsity into an equivariant Hamiltonian predictor. Two sparse gates selectively restrict interaction combinations judged non-critical, reducing the number of tensor-product computations while maintaining accuracy. A three-phase sparsity scheduler manages the sparse representation during training, supporting stable convergence and strong performance at sparsity levels reaching 70%.

On QH9 and PubchemQH, the authors report state-of-the-art accuracy and speedups of up to seven times over existing models. The results show that selectively reducing internal interactions can make this form of molecular prediction more computationally practical. The paper also identifies potential applications of the sparsification techniques to other SE(3)-equivariant networks; that broader usefulness is presented as a possibility beyond the demonstrated Hamiltonian task.
icml-2025-efficient-and-scalable-density.tldr: SPHNet selectively removes non-critical tensor interactions, achieving state-of-the-art Hamiltonian prediction accuracy with up to sevenfold speedups.

paragraphs: GERM targets the computational cost of adapting and compressing genomic foundation models. The paper identifies outliers as an obstacle to both low-rank adaptation and post-training quantization. Its approach is to remove those outliers through the model's attention mechanism, improving the practicality of genomic modeling when computational resources are scarce.

The authors replace standard attention with an outlier-free mechanism inspired by associative memory models. They apply outlier removal during pretraining and fine-tuning, reporting faster adaptation, lower computational costs, and more robust quantization within acceptable loss margins. A related strategy, GERM-T, uses small continual-learning steps to adapt existing checkpoints within this framework, avoiding the need to retrain from scratch.

The reported improvements over the baseline are 37.98% for fine-tuning performance and 64.34% for quantization. Average kurtosis falls by 92.14%, while the maximum infinity norm falls by 82.77%, providing additional evidence of reduced outlier behavior. The evaluations also report stronger performance than leading methods, supporting attention-level outlier removal as a practical route to more accessible genomic models.
icml-2025-fast-and-low-cost-genomic-foun.tldr: GERM uses outlier-free attention to improve genomic model adaptation and quantization, with a checkpoint-based strategy that avoids retraining from scratch.

paragraphs: Federated learning must combine updates from clients whose data can differ substantially, while also paying the cost of communicating those updates. FedSMU addresses both problems together. Its starting observation is that normalizing each update component's magnitude can reduce differences between client models caused by their different data, potentially improving the globally aggregated model's generalization.

The algorithm communicates symbols of client updates instead of their full magnitudes. It builds on the Lion optimizer by dividing its operation between local client updates and global server execution. This links the communication format directly to the optimization process: reducing the information transmitted is also intended to mitigate the effects of heterogeneous client data.

The authors prove convergence for general non-convex settings and evaluate FedSMU on several benchmark datasets. Those experiments show lower communication overhead alongside better generalization than the compression-based and optimization-based baselines compared. The contribution is therefore a coordinated treatment of communication and model heterogeneity, with both theoretical convergence support and empirical evidence for the combined benefit.
icml-2025-fedsmu-communication-efficient.tldr: FedSMU transmits symbolic client updates to reduce communication and improve generalization under heterogeneous federated data.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models are known for computational efficiency, but their behavior under memory constraints is less well understood. This paper asks how to choose between dense and expert-based models when both memory and computation are limited. The question matters because a configuration that looks efficient on computation alone may not be the best use of a fixed overall resource budget.

The authors develop joint scaling laws that account for active parameter count, training dataset size, and the number of experts. Bringing these factors into one framework allows the configuration decision to consider their combined effects. The resulting laws provide a principled way to select an MoE configuration under specified memory and compute budgets.

A central finding is that MoE models can be more memory-efficient than dense models, challenging the conventional expectation described in the paper. Extensive empirical evaluations support the scaling laws' predictions. The practical implication is conditional but useful: memory constraints need not rule out expert architectures, and model selection can be guided by the joint resource relationships.
icml-2025-joint-moe-scaling-laws-mixture.tldr: Joint scaling laws show how to configure mixture-of-experts models under fixed budgets and identify cases where they can be more memory-efficient than dense models.

paragraphs: KBQA-o1 answers natural-language questions using a structured knowledge base. The paper addresses three linked difficulties: language models may understand the knowledge base poorly, exploration can be costly, and training can depend heavily on annotated examples. Its approach turns answering into an agent process that explores the knowledge-base environment while constructing a logical form step by step.

The system uses a ReAct-based process together with Monte Carlo Tree Search. Policy and reward models guide this heuristic search, helping balance exploration quality against the size of the search space. The search also produces high-quality annotations that are used for incremental fine-tuning, connecting the answering procedure with further model improvement.

With limited annotated data, KBQA-o1 outperforms the previous low-resource methods evaluated. The reported GrailQA F1 score reaches 78.5% with Llama-3.1-8B, compared with 48.5% for the previous state-of-the-art method using GPT-3.5-turbo. This is a comparison between the reported systems and supports the usefulness of guided knowledge-base exploration and search-generated training annotations.
icml-2025-kbqa-o1-agentic-knowledge-base.tldr: KBQA-o1 combines stepwise knowledge-base exploration, tree search, and generated annotations to improve question answering with limited labeled data.

paragraphs: The simplex method solves linear programs by working from an initial basis, so choosing a useful starting basis can accelerate the solver. This paper emphasizes that resemblance to an optimal basis is not enough: a more accurate prediction does not always produce a larger speedup. The learning task therefore needs to address the practical quality of the starting point.

The authors propose a graph neural network using a three-part graph representation inspired by linear-programming duality. This representation is designed to improve feature extraction for general linear programs and make the network more expressive. They also introduce loss functions for selecting basic variables and encouraging basis feasibility, together with data preprocessing schemes.

These components aim to make predicted bases useful to the solver as well as accurate as predictions. Experiments report substantial improvements over the state-of-the-art method in basis-prediction accuracy, simplex iteration count, and solving time. The findings support evaluating learned warm starts through their downstream optimization benefits, with supervision that explicitly accounts for feasibility.
icml-2025-learning-initial-basis-selecti.tldr: A duality-inspired graph network learns feasible, useful simplex starting bases, improving prediction accuracy and reducing solver iterations and runtime.

paragraphs: An expected signature represents a collection of data streams through a feature tensor that can characterize the distribution generating those streams. This makes it useful for learning from time series without building a separate domain-specific model of the generating process. The paper focuses on the connection between that theoretical representation and the estimate actually computed from discretely observed data.

The authors prove convergence results linking the empirical discrete-time estimator with its continuous-time counterpart. This matters because practical learning methods operate on observations, while the probabilistic interpretation concerns an underlying process. Establishing the connection gives expected-signature methods a more complete account of what their estimated features represent.

The paper also considers the particular case where the generating process is a martingale. Under that condition, it proposes a simple estimator modification with substantially lower mean squared error. Empirical results show that the modification can improve predictive performance. This second contribution links a specific assumption about the data-generating process to a more accurate representation and demonstrated learning benefits.
icml-2025-learning-with-expected-signatu.tldr: The paper connects discrete expected-signature estimates to continuous-time theory and proposes a lower-error estimator for martingale data.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the structure of a forecasting Transformer matches its autoregressive task: predicting future values from earlier observations. The authors show that one linear-attention layer can be interpreted as a dynamic vector autoregressive model. That interpretation connects attention with a forecasting structure that describes relationships among multiple time series.

The difficulty arises when layers are stacked. The paper identifies structural mismatches in existing multilayer Transformers that obscure the underlying autoregressive form and impair interpretability and generalization. It shows that rearranging the multilayer perceptron, attention, and input-output flow allows multilayer linear attention to retain a vector autoregressive interpretation.

The resulting architecture, Structural Aligned Mixture of VAR, or SAMoVAR, incorporates interpretable dynamic VAR weights for multivariate forecasting. Compared with state-of-the-art forecasting models, the authors report improvements in prediction performance, interpretability, and computational efficiency. The contribution links architectural organization to the forecasting objective, showing how preserving an explicit autoregressive structure can support both understandable model behavior and stronger empirical results.
icml-2025-linear-transformers-as-var-mod.tldr: SAMoVAR reorganizes linear Transformers to preserve a vector autoregressive structure, improving multivariate forecasting, interpretability, and efficiency.

paragraphs: Text-based person re-identification commonly assumes that a witness supplies a complete description in one step. This paper instead starts from partial or vague descriptions and introduces interactive person re-identification. The system refines its retrieval query through a dialogue with the witness, making the acquisition of missing information part of the task itself.

To support this setting, the authors construct a dialogue dataset by breaking person descriptions into fine-grained attributes and incorporating several question types. Their LLaVA-ReID model uses both visual and textual context to generate targeted follow-up questions. The goal is to request additional details that are useful for identifying the intended person.

Training uses a looking-forward strategy to prioritize the most informative questions as supervision. This makes question selection an explicit learning objective, alongside the broader retrieval task. Experiments on both the new interactive benchmark and conventional text-based person re-identification benchmarks show significant improvements over the compared baselines. The findings support learning which details to ask for when the original description is incomplete.
icml-2025-llava-reid-selective-multi-ima.tldr: LLaVA-ReID learns informative follow-up questions to refine incomplete person descriptions and improve retrieval through dialogue.

paragraphs: Distributed mixture-of-experts models can spend a large share of runtime moving information between devices. The paper reports that this communication consumes over 40% of runtime in large-scale training. Occult studies this bottleneck through pairs of experts activated by the same token, distinguishing pairs located on one device from pairs spread across devices.

Initial investigations show that increasing the share of same-device collaboration can accelerate expert parallelism. Occult builds system-level and algorithm-level methods around that observation. Its designs offer two distinct options: reduce communication while preserving exact results, or use collaboration pruning and modified fine-tuning to reduce communication costs in a controlled way.

Experiments across multiple mixture-of-experts language models and tasks report speedups exceeding 50% over popular state-of-the-art training or inference frameworks. Quality is comparable to or better than standard fine-tuning in the reported evaluations. The work shows how the relationships among co-activated experts can guide communication optimization, with separate choices for exact computation and changes supported by fine-tuning.
icml-2025-occult-optimizing-collaborativ.tldr: Occult reduces communication among co-activated experts, reporting over 50% speedups across multiple MoE tasks and models.

paragraphs: PathConv explores whether an image-processing network can rely entirely on one-dimensional operations while retaining strong accuracy. Such operations offer parameter efficiency, but simply flattening an image can separate pixels that are neighbors in two dimensions. The paper treats preservation of these local relationships as the central design problem.

The authors analyze Hilbert and Z-order traversal paths and identify a trade-off: improving proximity for most pixels can leave some neighboring pixels excessively far apart. Their path-shifting method changes which pixels suffer that separation. Using randomized rounding, they show that three shifted paths are sufficient to preserve locality better than straightforward raster scanning.

Combining several paths can introduce convergence difficulties, so the model includes lightweight path-aware channel attention. This mechanism captures local dependencies within paths and global dependencies across paths. Experiments report ResNet-level accuracy with one-third of the parameters and support the effectiveness of the proposed components. The result establishes one-dimensional path processing as a viable approach to building efficient vision backbones.
icml-2025-one-dimensional-path-convoluti.tldr: PathConv combines shifted image traversal paths and path-aware attention to achieve ResNet-level accuracy using one-third of the parameters.

paragraphs: A vision-language model may answer from familiar associations in its training data instead of examining the image carefully. This paper investigates that possibility with ViLP, a benchmark containing deliberately out-of-distribution generated images and question-answer pairs. Its design separates cases where text-based expectations suffice from cases that require visual reasoning.

Each question has three possible answers and three corresponding images: one permits an answer from text priors alone, while two require visual reasoning. Humans achieve nearly perfect accuracy, but the evaluated models struggle; GPT-4o scores 66.17%. The contrast provides evidence that the benchmark exposes weaknesses in how these models use visual information.

The authors also propose a self-improvement procedure in which models create new visual question-answering data. Pixel-level and semantic corruptions produce good-bad image pairs for training. An objective called Image-DPO encourages greater reliance on the actual visual input, with effectiveness demonstrated in LLaVA-v1.5 and Cambrian. The paper thus combines a diagnostic benchmark with a training approach aimed at the behavior it exposes.
icml-2025-probing-visual-language-priors.tldr: ViLP exposes weaknesses in visual reasoning, while Image-DPO uses corrupted image pairs to encourage models to attend to visual evidence.

paragraphs: This paper develops quantum algorithms for time-dependent decision problems with a finite planning horizon. It studies two access settings separately: full knowledge of transition probabilities, and a generative model that supplies environment samples in quantum superposition. These access assumptions determine what information the algorithms can use and are central to the claimed advantages.

With exact dynamics, QVI-1 computes an optimal policy and value function with a quadratic improvement in action-space dependence over classical value iteration. QVI-2 obtains near-optimal policies and values with an additional improvement in state-space dependence. Both algorithms have quantum query complexities that improve on classical lower bounds, particularly in their dependence on state and action counts.

With quantum-superposition sampling access, QVI-3 and QVI-4 improve sample complexity relative to the state-of-the-art classical algorithm in action count, estimation error, and horizon dependence. Quantum lower bounds show these two algorithms are asymptotically optimal up to logarithmic factors when the horizon is constant. The results establish resource-complexity advantages within the specified quantum access settings.
icml-2025-quantum-algorithms-for-finite-.tldr: Four quantum value-iteration algorithms improve finite-horizon planning complexity under exact-dynamics or quantum-sampling access assumptions.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires a model to acquire new knowledge while preserving what it learned earlier. These goals are often described as plasticity and stability. This paper argues that network architecture deserves attention alongside parameter-level learning methods, because the shape of a network can influence how well it serves each goal.

Under an equal parameter budget, the authors find that deeper networks show better plasticity, whereas wider networks show better stability. Dual-Arch uses these complementary tendencies in two distinct, independent networks. One has a lightweight architecture specialized for learning new information, while the other has a lightweight architecture specialized for preserving previous knowledge.

The framework is designed as a plug-in for existing continual-learning methods. Extensive experiments show improved performance while using up to 87% fewer parameters. The findings make architecture an additional means of managing the stability-plasticity trade-off: separately designed networks can serve the two objectives more effectively in the evaluated settings, without requiring a larger overall parameter footprint.
icml-2025-rethinking-the-stability-plast.tldr: Dual-Arch pairs architectures specialized for learning and retention, improving continual-learning methods while being up to 87% smaller.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders aim to represent data using a compact set of active latent features. This paper revisits their ability to capture low-dimensional structure, including natural-image structure and patterns in language-model activations. The authors formalize weaknesses in conventional sparse autoencoders and in related variational autoencoders applied to these tasks, then propose a hybrid alternative.

The theoretical result concerns global minima of the proposed model: they recover certain forms of structured data distributed across a union of manifolds. The qualification matters because the guarantee applies to specified data structures and global solutions. It provides a formal connection between the model's objective and recovery of the underlying structure.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data support more accurate estimates of manifold dimensions and sparser latent representations without worsening reconstruction error. The authors report stronger performance than equal-capacity sparse and variational autoencoders, and than recent diffusion models where applicable. Across images and language-model activation patterns, the results support revisiting the modeling recipe behind sparse representations.
icml-2025-sparse-autoencoders-again-990c.tldr: A hybrid autoencoder improves latent sparsity and manifold estimation, with structured-data recovery guarantees at global minima.

paragraphs: Unsupervised graph domain adaptation uses labeled graphs from one domain to make predictions in another domain without target labels. SLOGAN addresses the difficulty of separating useful, stable features from correlations that depend on the source domain. The paper also identifies shortcomings in global alignment strategies when transferring graph representations across distribution shifts.

The method first builds a sparse causal graph. Mutual-information bottleneck constraints and variational inference aim to isolate stable causal features while compressing domain-dependent correlations. It then recombines features across domains through a generative intervention mechanism to break remaining local spurious couplings. Covariance constraints preserve the semantic consistency of causal features during this process.

SLOGAN also introduces category-adaptive dynamic calibration to reduce the accumulation of errors in target-domain pseudo-labels. This addresses the supervision used during adaptation alongside the representation being transferred. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report significant improvements over existing baselines. The findings support combining sparse causal modeling, feature interventions, and calibrated pseudo-labels for more stable graph transfer in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-sparse-causal-discovery-with-g.tldr: SLOGAN combines sparse causal modeling, cross-domain feature interventions, and pseudo-label calibration to improve unsupervised graph transfer.

paragraphs: Many neurons in a language model's feed-forward networks contribute only weakly, creating opportunities to avoid unnecessary computation. This paper studies activation sparsity quantitatively: how to measure it, how architecture and training affect it, and how those findings can guide the construction of more efficient models. It introduces CETT-PPL-1% as a generalizable, performance-friendly measurement.

Using that metric, the authors observe a convergent power-law relationship between sparsity and the amount of training data. They also find greater sparsity capability with ReLU than with the widely used SiLU activation, potential benefits from a smaller width-to-depth ratio, and insensitivity of activation sparsity to model scale. These are reported observations from the study.

The authors apply the findings to train a 2.4-billion-parameter model with a sparsity ratio of 93.52%. It achieves a 4.1-fold speedup relative to its dense version. This demonstration connects the measurement and architectural analysis to practical acceleration, showing how deliberate choices during model development can support highly sparse activation.
icml-2025-sparsing-law-towards-large-lan.tldr: A quantitative study of activation sparsity guides a 2.4-billion-parameter model with 93.52% sparsity and a 4.1-fold speedup over its dense version.

paragraphs: An optimizer's choice of geometry affects which update direction counts as steepest. This paper notes that widely used methods such as SGD, AdamW, and Lion rely on steepest-descent updates associated with either the l2 or l-infinity norm. It investigates a broader family of l-p geometries to address non-Euclidean structure encountered in deep-network training.

The proposed optimizer, Stacey, is an accelerated l-p steepest-descent algorithm. It uses interpolated primal and dual iterate sequences to navigate smooth optimization problems in this geometry. The authors provide theoretical guarantees for the algorithm's foundations, connecting the update design with an analysis of nonconvex optimization.

Experiments compare Stacey with SGD, AdamW, and Lion on image classification and language-model pretraining, reporting faster convergence and higher final accuracy. The study also varies p across models and datasets, examining how the choice of geometry affects training. These results support treating the norm underlying steepest descent as a useful optimization choice, with empirical benefits for the tasks evaluated.
icml-2025-stacey-promoting-stochastic-st.tldr: Stacey extends accelerated steepest descent to l-p geometries, reporting faster convergence and higher accuracy in image classification and language-model pretraining.

paragraphs: Reducing image tokens can lower the arithmetic cost of attention in diffusion models, but it does not automatically shorten generation time. This paper identifies sorting and scattered writes as sources of overhead in earlier token-merging methods. Those costs can cancel theoretical savings when the model already uses optimized attention implementations such as FlashAttention.

ToMA redesigns token reduction around operations that GPUs execute efficiently. It formulates token selection as a submodular optimization problem to choose diverse tokens, then expresses merging and unmerging as attention-like linear transformations using matrix operations. It also uses latent locality and reuses patterns across sequential computation to reduce additional overhead.

The method is intended for off-the-shelf use. Reported generation latency falls by 24% for SDXL and 23% for Flux, with DINO changes below 0.07, outperforming prior methods. The contribution is the connection between token-reduction design and actual execution costs: the measured benefit comes from making the reduction procedure efficient enough to preserve its savings during image generation.
icml-2025-toma-token-merge-with-attentio.tldr: ToMA uses GPU-friendly token merging to reduce SDXL and Flux generation latency by 24% and 23%, respectively.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how a single autoregressive vision-language model represents the many tasks it can perform. The authors find that conceptually equivalent inputs align into a shared task vector across text and images, and across instructions and examples. Such a representation may simplify the model's processing by expressing task information in a common internal form.

They test this alignment through cross-modal transfer: a task vector obtained in one modality is used to trigger the appropriate generation in another. Across a range of tasks and model architectures, the highly compressed vector outperforms supplying the full task information in the prompt. The authors identify this advantage specifically in the cross-modal setting.

They also show that task vectors can transfer from a base language model to its fine-tuned vision-language counterpart. Vectors can be derived from instructions alone, without examples. Together, the findings provide evidence that models represent task meaning in ways that extend across input modalities and formats, offering a clearer view of their internal organization.
icml-2025-vision-language-models-create-.tldr: Vision-language models form shared task vectors that transfer across text and images and can outperform full prompts in cross-modal tasks.
